7: Part one: the body. The whole idea of Count Yourself Skinny fits in one line: you'll never count a calorie — you'll count to 32 instead. Naturally lean people aren't doing math on food labels. Watch one eat: one bite, fork down, they chew a long time, they stop when they're comfortable. It's mechanics, not arithmetic.
8: In a small Iowa State University study of 45 adults, people who chewed 50 percent more ate about 10 percent less at a single lab lunch. Those who doubled their chews ate about 15 percent less. Same pizza, same table — they just stopped sooner, and they weren't any hungrier. The reason is timing: fullness signals take a while to build. A fast eater finishes the plate before the signal arrives. Honest note, and it's in the book: it was one meal, not a diet, and chewing is one lever in a stack — which brings us to the other counts.
9: Here's the whole program on one slide. Six easy numbers instead of calories: 32 chews per bite. 2,500 steps a day — that's the floor, not the goal. 12 hours between dinner and breakfast, working up to 14 or 16 if it feels good, and 3 hours between your last bite and bed. 10 minutes of morning light, outside, no sunglasses, within an hour of waking. 2 glasses of water before noon, the first before your coffee. And nights of 7-plus hours — shoot for 7 out of 7. No food scale. No forbidden foods. Nothing to buy.
10: Quick story about 10,000 steps: that number traces to a Japanese business slogan and walking clubs from the 1960s. The real research is much friendlier. A pooled analysis of 17 studies and nearly 227,000 adults found the heart benefit showing up around 2,300 steps a day and the all-cause benefit around 3,900. Every extra 500 steps was linked to about 7 percent fewer heart-related deaths. The point: going from zero to something is worth more than going from good to great. You don't need to be an athlete. You need to start counting.
11: This is my favorite part of the book. One morning walk — about 25 minutes, before breakfast — checks five boxes at once. Your steps are banked before the day can get in the way. You get your morning light. Your overnight fast keeps going. That morning light helps you fall asleep tonight. And you drink one glass of water before you leave and one when you get back. Shoes by the door tonight. Out the door within an hour of waking. That's the whole program in twenty-five minutes.
12: And here's what makes it stick. Every evening, one yes-or-no question: did I hit my counts today? If yes, the streak grows by one. That's the whole tracking system. You will miss days — life happens. One missed day is a rest. Two in a row is a new habit forming in the wrong direction. So guard the day after a miss like it's the whole program, because it is. There's a free printable Count Log on the website if you want to track it on paper.

14: Part two: the brain. You heard me say it at the start; this is the book it comes from. Begin with the End in Mind, and the subtitle is the whole reason I do this: don't lose your identity and your dignity while you still have a choice.
15: Here's the line I want everyone to remember, whether you're 25 or 75: Alzheimer's is a disease that shows up when you're older. It starts in midlife. According to the Alzheimer's Association, changes in the brain can begin 20 years or more before the first symptom. Which means the window to do something about it isn't at 75. It's now. For the younger people in the room — this is exactly why you start now, while it's easy.
16: Most people believe dementia is genetics and bad luck — and if it's inevitable, why bother? That belief is the single biggest reason people do nothing for decades. The research says otherwise. The Lancet Commission — the most respected review in the field — concluded in 2024 that up to 45 percent of dementia cases may be preventable or delayed by addressing modifiable risk factors.
17: These are the 14 modifiable risk factors from the Lancet Commission. You don't control your genes. You do control a lot of these. And notice how many connect back to what we just talked about: physical inactivity, obesity, diabetes, blood pressure, cholesterol, even sleep and mood. The chew count isn't really about your waistline. It's the first domino.
18: Fourteen risk factors is a lot to carry around in your head. So I put them in four buckets — the 4M System. Mind is the destination. Muscle is the engine. Mitigate removes the harm. And Motivate makes it stick, because knowing isn't the hard part; doing it for years is. Every risk factor fits in one of these four buckets.

24: Look at this list. Your house burns down — your carrier writes the check. A wreck where you're at fault — carrier. You die early — life insurance. You can't work — disability. A stay in the hospital — health insurance. Ten years of dementia care? You do. That's the one line on the list where the check comes out of your family's pocket.
25: This is the part that surprises every room. Medicare does not pay for custodial long-term care. The memory care bill, the in-home aide, the assisted living community — that's almost entirely private pay, until you've spent down to Medicaid eligibility. And the private long-term-care insurance market has largely collapsed; very few carriers still sell new standalone policies.
26: Here's what a decade can look like, one stage at a time. Stage one, early: doctor visits, medications, home safety changes, legal and financial planning — about 35 to 40 thousand. Stage two: the spouse can't do it alone anymore — a paid caregiver 20 hours a week plus adult day care — about 170 to 180 thousand. Stage three: 24/7 supervision. Memory care runs about $8,000 a month nationally — about 290 to 340 thousand. Add it up: roughly half a million dollars over ten years. The Alzheimer's Association's own figure, the average lifetime cost of care for one person with dementia, is $405,262 — and 70 percent of it is carried by the family. Our scenario lands right on top of the national data.
27: Two numbers to remember. The first is $405,000 — the average lifetime cost when one person develops dementia, with 70 percent of it coming out of the family's pocket. The second is 63 percent — that's how much higher the death rate is for a strained spouse who becomes the caregiver. This diagnosis doesn't take one life. It taxes two.
28: So here's the reframe. You can't buy your way out of this risk anymore. But you can underwrite it: know the number, and work on what's in your control. Nothing prevents dementia outright, and I'll never tell you it does. But the evidence says the odds can move — and the premium is about ten hours a month, two and a half hours a week, spent on the habits we've talked about tonight.
